opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly one I struggled with myself.

Early in a PhD, the first papers are mostly about learning the craft: how to pick a problem small enough to finish, how to run experiments carefully, how to write so reviewers understand you. That stage matters, and you shouldn't skip it. But at some point you realize that a stream of papers that each get cited a few dozen times doesn't add up to impact on its own.

So my first piece of advice is to **look for the pattern behind your papers.** After two or three projects, ask yourself: what kept slowing me down? What did I have to rebuild from scratch every time? For me, that question led directly to Taichi. I was doing physical simulation and graphics research, and I kept writing the same messy, high-performance code over and over. Eventually it felt more valuable to solve that underlying pain than to write one more simulation paper. Very often the pain you feel is shared by many other people, and that's where broader impact comes from.

Second, **think about who uses your work, not only who cites it.** A paper is a message to a small community of experts. A tool, a library, a dataset, or a clean open-source implementation can reach thousands of people, many of whom will never read your paper. That takes a different kind of effort: documentation, examples, answering GitHub issues, caring about installation. Academia doesn't always reward that directly, but it compounds over time.

Third, **be willing to take a bigger, riskier bet once you have some foundation.** Your first papers give you credibility and confidence. Use that to work on something that might take a couple of years and might not fit neatly into one conference deadline. Talk to your advisor about it honestly. A good advisor will support you if you can explain why it matters.

Finally, **stay close to real users and real problems.** Impact isn't something you can plan purely from the top down. You put something out, people try it, they tell you what's broken, and you iterate. That feedback loop is humbling, but it's also how a research idea becomes something people actually rely on.

So the transition is really a shift in mindset: from "What can I publish next?" to "What problem, if I solved it well, would make many other people's work easier?" Once you start asking that question, the papers tend to follow naturally.

r001.rationale: It says early papers help students learn research and writing, but does not advise prioritizing publication over discerning industry trends.

r002.rationale: After two or three projects, it advises looking for the pattern behind the papers and identifying what they have in common.

r003.rationale: It treats use of tools and other work as a sign of reach, but does not mention adoption by people in other fields.

r004.rationale: It says early papers build craft, credibility, and confidence, but does not explain that early execution supplies information needed for broader impact.

r005.rationale: It advises finding a problem that would help many people, but does not advise students with a publication record to reflect on why they pursue research.

r006.rationale: It does not claim that ten times the impact can be achieved with only twice the effort.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That's a question I think about a lot, because I went through that transition myself and honestly didn't handle it perfectly.

When you publish your first paper or two, there's a very natural pull to keep doing the same thing. You've found a little niche, you know the reviewers, you know what the next incremental step is, and the reward loop is fast. I don't want to dismiss that phase. You need to learn how to finish things, how to write, how to deal with rejection. Those first papers teach you that. But at some point you have to ask a different question, which is not "what's the next paper" but "what would actually change how people work if it existed?"

For me that shift happened with Taichi. I was doing graphics simulation research, and I kept noticing that the bottleneck wasn't ideas, it was that every idea took weeks of painful low-level code to try. So instead of writing the fifth simulation paper, I asked whether I could remove that pain for everyone, including myself. That's a riskier bet. It's slower to publish, and it's not obvious which conference it belongs in. But the impact compounds in a way a single paper never does, because other people build on it.

So my concrete advice would be a few things.

First, pay attention to your own frustrations. If something is annoying you repeatedly in your research workflow, it's probably annoying a thousand other people. That frustration is a research direction in disguise.

Second, build things people can actually use. Release the code, write documentation, answer issues on GitHub. A lot of students treat that as a distraction from "real" research. I'd argue the opposite. The moment real users touch your work, you learn what matters and what doesn't, and that feedback is far more honest than a reviewer's.

Third, be patient with yourself and talk to your advisor about the tradeoff openly. Broader impact usually means fewer papers in the short term. That's okay if you're deliberate about it, but it shouldn't be an accident.

And finally, think about who you're really serving. Early on, your audience is a handful of reviewers. Later, it should be practitioners, other researchers, maybe people outside your field entirely. Once you start writing and building for that larger audience, the kind of problems you choose naturally changes. That's really the whole transition in one sentence.

r001.rationale: The response says first papers teach students how to finish and write, but does not advise prioritizing publication over discerning industry trends.

r002.rationale: It does not advise students with several strong papers to assess whether those papers form a coherent body of work.

r003.rationale: It encourages serving a broader audience and building usable tools, but does not propose adoption by people in other fields as a measure of impact.

r004.rationale: It mentions lessons from early papers, but does not explain that intensive early execution provides information needed to pursue broader impact later.

r005.rationale: It recommends considering what would change how people work and whom the research serves, but does not give the specified advice to students with an established publication record to spend time reflecting on why they pursue their research.

r006.rationale: The response does not suggest that ten times the impact could require only twice the effort.

astra-6.text:
I think your first paper is an important milestone because it teaches you how to turn an idea into a result that other researchers can understand and evaluate. But as you gain experience, it helps to shift from asking, “What can I publish?” to asking, “What problem is worth spending the next few years on?”

A paper can be one step toward solving that problem. The next step might be building a system people can use, making your code easier to reproduce, or talking to people whose needs challenge your assumptions. Those activities give you feedback that you may not get from the review process.

I wouldn’t put pressure on students to have a huge impact immediately. Start with something concrete, do it well, and pay attention to what happens after publication. Does someone build on it? Does it help someone do something they couldn’t do before? That can guide your next research question and help you develop a direction that extends beyond a single paper.

r001.rationale: It calls the first paper an important milestone but does not advise prioritizing publication over discerning industry trends.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss whether several strong papers form a coherent body of work.

r003.rationale: It mentions whether someone builds on or benefits from a paper, but not adoption by people in other fields.

r004.rationale: It recommends concrete work and learning from feedback, but does not say intensive early PhD execution supplies information for broader impact later.

r005.rationale: For students gaining experience, it recommends shifting from asking what they can publish to considering what problem is worth pursuing for the next few years.

r006.rationale: It does not compare the effort needed with achieving ten times the research impact.

sol-6.1.text:
I think your first paper is an important milestone because it teaches you how to do research: how to formulate a question, test an idea, and communicate the result. But after that, it helps to step back and ask, “If this research succeeds, who will care, and what will they be able to do that they couldn’t do before?”

That question can change how you choose problems. You might spend more time building a system people can actually use, talking to potential users, or understanding why an existing approach hasn’t been adopted. Those activities may not immediately produce another paper, but they can reveal much more meaningful research questions.

I wouldn’t treat publishing and impact as two completely separate stages. Keep developing your research skills while finding ways to put your ideas in contact with reality. Release code, get feedback, and pay attention to where people struggle. A paper gives you a way to explain an idea; seeing someone use it gives you a different kind of evidence that the idea matters.

r001.rationale: The response discusses what to do after a first paper; it does not advise students without one to prioritize publication over discerning industry trends.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss students with several strong papers or whether their work forms a coherent body of research.

r003.rationale: It suggests seeing whether people use a system, but does not identify adoption by people in other fields as a measure of impact.

r004.rationale: It does not say that intensive early PhD execution provides information needed to pursue broader impact later.

r005.rationale: It encourages reflection after a first paper about who might care and what the research could enable, but does not address students with an established publication record or clearly advise them to consider why they pursue research.

r006.rationale: The response makes no claim that ten times the impact can require only twice the effort.
